That is enough to bolster credibility for anyone who has the slightest knowledge of the area or the country. The landscape could not be more accurate from the actual.

Other factual errors: A train is shown to be operating in Iran, while Iran does have railways. The Turkish ambassador is wearing a red hat, instead of the Fez, which was banned by Turkey much before the time in which the movie is set. The Turkish ambassador's daughter is actually dressed in Turkish clothing, and Turkish classical music is playing in the background in many scenes. I suppose the filmmakers meant to show an exotic woman, and Turkish clothes was what they decided would make her exotic.

So I flipped on the digital subscriber channels one night a couple of years ago and thought I'd pass a half hour watching "Girlfight" while waiting for "Hart's War" to start. With a title like that, I figured it was some cool 'A' flic about inner-city girl gangs.

Much to my surprise, it wasn't about that at all. Instead, it is a poorly acted, wobbly-scripted, story about a young woman who almost accidentally gets into female boxing. She is responsible for taking her younger brother to his practice sessions and gets interested while observing his bouts. As he doesn't really want to be a boxer (only following through on their father's wishes) she convinces his coach to take her on in his stead.

The story unfolds in an unintelligent and unbelievable way as she goes through various trials on her quest. For starters, her brother's coach doesn't want to take on a female boxer. After grudgingly doing so there is the problem of lining up matches for her. Then the confrontation with her father when he finds out what is going on. Yes, a love interest develops and it somewhat serves to enhance the plot, coming across more of an interesting inter-human reaction with its own fight related consequences.

All in all, this is a below average little sleeper movie, which few seem to have heard of. Sometime later, when I saw the much advertised and acclaimed "Million Dollar Baby" I thought "wait a minute, this seems kind of familiar". Needless to say, I definitely watched "Hart's War" that night.

text:
I went into The Straight Story expecting a sad/happy type drama with nice direction and some good acting. These I didn't get. What I wasn't expecting was an allegory for the trials of human existence. Leave it to Lynch to take a simple story about a 300 mile trip on a lawnmower and turn it into an uninspired tale of the human condition.

If you didn't notice, don't watch it again, pay no attention to the ages of the people Alvin meets, the terrain he's driving through, the reactions people give him, the kinds of discussions he has (one of the first is about pregnancy and children, one of the last is outside of a cemetery). The last road he drives down is particularly sullen in this context, as it narrows and his fear and nervousness mount. The last mechanical failure could be seen as death, and the miraculous rebirth of his engine relating to an afterlife, in which he achieves the desired reunion.

I agree with the people who branded this as a slow sappy melodrama.

This film is about a man who has been too caught up with the accepted convention of success, trying to be ever upwardly mobile, working hard so that he could be proud of owning his own home. He assumes this is all there is to life until he accidentally takes up dancing, all because he wanted to get a closer look of a beautiful girl that he sees by the dance studio everyday while riding the subway on his way home.

His was infatuated with her at first, going to the dance class just to idolize her, but he eventually lets himself go and gets himself into the dancing. It eventually becomes apparent to him that there is more to life than working yourself to death. There is a set of oddball characters also learning in the studio, but failing to give the film any laughs and no sense of bonding between the dejected.

There are no revelations of the various characters, especially the girl he initially admired, prohibiting any depth to them by not showing their blemished past and their struggle to overcome it.

The dancing also wasn't engaging, with the big competition at the end, but it is the usual story where our underdog comes out at the top by winning it. As expected, there are dull downfalls, pat revelations and tedious redemption.

All these make it a boring and feckless film to watch.

Jon Voight is awful in Midnight Cowboy, but Hoffman's performance, though reminiscent of his later turn in Rainman, is the kind of performance that keeps me hating movies. As a portrayal of a New York character, only Daniel Day Lewis' portrayal of Bill Butcher in Gangs of New York comes to mind as comparable, and Day doesn't give his character the emotional depth that Hoffman gives Ratso.

It's typical of Hoffman's way of acting that the actor we tend to identify most with Midnight Cowboy is Voight. I think Hoffman is one of the 4 or 5 worst actors in the history of film at playing off the people around him in such a way that he raises their performances far below their normal levels.

Voight's Buck is so naive that he would float out of the film altogether, except that Ratso pulls him down - pulls him down, but also teaches him, a lot about how to survive and, more importantly, how to live.

Midnight Cowboy is a movie about escape that turns into a movie about finding yourself. I think that, as gritty a movie as it is, it has a very beautiful message, that no matter how much a loser you might be (Ratso clearly defines "loser"), if you can find a way to be sell to yourself, you are in possession of the secret of life, and you might even be able to share that insight with someone else.

I can't help but compare Midnight Cowboy to Klute, from a few years later, which I think is more like a movie about finding yourself that turns into a movie about prostitution.

Jon Voight delivers a unique performance in Midnight Cowboy, and Hoffman's portrayal, reminiscent of his later turn in Rainman, is the kind of performance that reminds me why I love movies. It's a testament to Hoffman's acting style that the actor we tend to associate most with Midnight Cowboy is Voight. Hoffman has a rare ability to play off the people around him in such a way that he elevates their performances far beyond their usual levels.  

Voight's Buck is so naive that he might drift through the film untouched, but Ratso grounds him—grounds him, and also teaches him invaluable lessons about survival and, more importantly, about truly living.

As gritty as the movie is, it carries a profoundly beautiful message: no matter how much of an outsider you might feel like (Ratso clearly embodies the "outsider"), if you can find a way to connect with yourself, you hold the secret to life, and you might even be able to share that

Sunshine is a European import set in Hungary between 1880 and 1980, it's the epic story of Hungarian Jews, the Sonnenschein family. This name literally translates to Sunshine. The family has humble beginnings, then is prosperous, becomes upwardly mobile, changes it's name, and hopes to assimilate into Hungarian society so successive generations can advance professionally. The story is told through the eyes of the eldest son in each of three generations; Ralph Fiennes plays these three roles. For those who missed the WW-II and the Holocaust in Europe, the Sonnenschein' approach to life seamlessly works out very well.

Sunshine is being acclaimed as an artistic success. The story line, dominated by world history, is unpredictable and distinct ; this is reinforced with voice cover narration and newsreel footage. The family 'plot' lurches from one unpredictable event [ie. the Hapsburgs, WW-I, WW-II, Fascism, Communism, etc.] to the next with continuity, depth and much detail. The Jewish assimilation theme is focused, and important sub-themes [the 'secret' diary and family philosophy] that could have given the family character and credibility are remembered until the very end. Alternatively, the filmmakers provide generation continuity using common themes of incest / infidelity.

Ralph Fiennes exhibits flashes of brilliance, his performance is award winning material. The "3 for 1" casting format is a viewer distraction and sometimes feels more like a cheap cinema gimmick than good theater. Sunshine is basically Hungarian "History Channel" material. Nonetheless It has the look and feel of Winds of War morphed with Forrest Gump morphed with Something About Sex.

The great, iconic Leslie Cheung plays a tax collector hero who stays the night in a haunted temple and gets involved with a captivating fox spirit and a lively Taoist. Cheung's performance is filled with naive yet dignified charm, and Wu Ma is delightfully eccentric as the Taoist monk, who showcases some swordplay and even gets a musical number. Joey Wang, as the fox spirit, brings a memorable presence, with every movement and gesture adding to the mystical allure. The film blends elements of fantasy, horror, comedy, and romance, all stirred together into a consistently entertaining package. Ching Siu Tung, directing and handling the choreography, delivers impressive wirework thrills and fills the film with mists, shadows, and eerily enchanting forest colors, giving every forest scene a mesmerizing atmosphere. Back in his youth, the old man had entertained the unsettling idea of marrying his first cousin, but his family rightly forbade it. Many decades later, the old man has raised three children (two boys and one girl), and shockingly allows his son and daughter to marry and have children. Before long, the sister grows tired of brother #1 and disgracefully moves on to brother #2.

One might hope that the three siblings are isolated on a remote island, far from society. But no -- they are upper-class Europeans attending college and mingling in the social world.

Not once do we witness any interest from the brothers toward non-related females. Not once do we see the sister showing any interest in non-related males. Every romantic or flirtatious interaction is disturbingly confined to the siblings themselves.

The most unsettling part of GLADIATOR was the incestuous undertone. The young emperor Commodus, surrounded by countless slave girls and a city full of potential matches, fixated solely on his sister. If movie incest makes you uncomfortable, then SUNSHINE will (painfully) drag you through its slow and awkward narrative.

Sunshine is a European import set in Hungary between 1880 and 1980, attempting to tell the sprawling story of Hungarian Jews, the Sonnenschein family. This name literally translates to Sunshine. The family starts with modest beginnings, rises to prosperity, becomes socially ambitious, changes its name, and tries to assimilate into Hungarian society, all in the hope that successive generations can climb the professional ladder. The story is narrated through the eldest son in each of three generations; Ralph Fiennes portrays all three roles, though this casting choice feels forced and overly contrived. For those unfamiliar with WW-II and the Holocaust in Europe, the Sonnenschein family's approach to life seems overly simplistic and detached from reality.

Sunshine is being discussed as an artistic attempt, but its execution falters. The storyline, heavily influenced by world history, is chaotic and lacks coherence; this is compounded by voiceover narration and scattered newsreel footage. The family’s trajectory stumbles from one disjointed historical event [ie. the Hapsburgs, WW-I, WW-II, Fascism, Communism, etc.] to the next, with excessive detail that often feels overwhelming rather than insightful. Love screwball comedy? Edel & Starck might just be your next favorite. If you're looking for something different from the typical lawyers' drama like Law & Order, this show offers a refreshing take. (Though Law & Order is undeniably brilliant in its own right, but I digress.) E&S brings light-hearted humor, romance, and wit to the table, creating an enjoyable and entertaining experience.

Honestly, the series wrapped up at the right time, leaving a lasting impression without overstaying its welcome. It's encouraging to see private German television productions exploring unique storytelling approaches. German residents will know what I mean.

In short: Give it a watch. I can't speak for the English synchronization, but hey, it’s worth diving in for its four seasons of fun. A cheerful ending awaits.

text: Incarcerated train robber near Yuma escapes his chain-gang and heads for the retired sheriff responsible for killing his wife (as well as a hidden stash of gold which remains hidden due to a contrived script). The attempt to modernize the western genre with 1970s-style violence and brutality feels forced and overly grim, leaving it as just another forgettable entry among the late-'90s westerns. It struggles to hold interest, with the female characters poorly utilized and barely making an impact. As the former sheriff back in command, Charlton Heston delivers one of his more lackluster performances (he has an awkward moment fumbling with a letter and his glasses). James Coburn, as the half-mad half-breed, comes across as over-the-top, and his attempts to elevate the basic dialogue and situations often fall flat. It’s a tedious watch all the way. 1.5 out of ****

A retired diplomat, played stiffly by Michael York, goes to Russia to seek revenge on the Russian gangster who murdered the diplomat's policeman son. There, the diplomat meets a rather bland and unremarkable Russian cop who somehow helps him bring the gangster to justice.

It reminded me of the old, over-the-top action flicks of the 1980s that always portrayed Russians as cartoonishly evil villains. This time, they try to flip the script with a Russian hero, but it doesn’t really work.

Not a great flick, and honestly, it barely rises above the level of a generic "B" action movie. Michael York tries his best to elevate the material, but even his presence can't save this uninspired mess. Alexander Nevsky, who plays the Russian cop, is wooden and lacks charisma, though he awkwardly manages some forced chemistry with York. Let’s face it, Michael York is such a seasoned actor that he could probably create chemistry with a brick wall. Frustratingly, the only other actor with any real presence, Adrian Paul, is killed off within the first 15 minutes of the movie. If Adrian Paul had stuck around longer, maybe the film would’ve been slightly less tedious. As it stands

Brigitte Nielsen’s transformation from her futuristic-nurse look (so striking!) to the iconic high-top fade we remember from Beverly Hills Cop II was a delightful revelation.

text:
The acting was great, the story was full of turns and complex characters. It's about the repercussions of the struggle between right-wing Flemish block voters on the one side and the Moroccon people living in the Belgian city Antwerp on the other side. Is it a political analysis ? Is it some kind of Belgian West Side Story or modern Romeo and Juliet ? The film just isn't strong enough to answer both questions (supposing those were the director's questions, too). Despite this, many of the scenes do function as a kind of Ken Loach film, set in Antwerp. After all, this city has been the starting point of the extremist right-wing Flemish Block party and is struggling with a lot of problems and tensions between different populations and cultures. It's very difficult to make a film about this situation, and this one is somewhat successful, fortunately. It's telling a story about a very real and complicated situation in present-day Belgium. The few foreign viewers watching should try and enjoy it and realise it's not the actual film that is important but the social dividing lines behind it that haunt Belgium, a 10 million people country, in the 2000s

It's mind boggling how anyone could have created this masterpiece. Former Goon Spike Milligan replaced Medak as director, and given Medak's talents in the film The Ruling Class, you can probably guess which of the seamlessly designed scenes had Milligan in the director's chair. Peter Boyle makes a brief appearance in the film's first 10 minutes as the doomed pirate captain. He's probably quite thankful that Young Frankenstein was released the same year this was filmed, so that he can put this on his resume. Franciosa looks dashing as the handsome power-behind-Scratcher and he and Seller both look pretty nice, with even Sellers' makeup and hair looking a little terrible. They had to know this movie was to be a hit even as they were filming it. With lines like these, I can understand any possible awards. PIERRE: (about to be hanged) You'll pay for this. SCRATCHER: No, I won't. I'll do it for free.  That's one of the good jokes. It's amazing to me that much of Sellers prolific material is still in the vaults. This was made available on VHS more than 15 years ago! How about someone stepping up to the plate and releasing in the US the well-received British TV program "A Show Called Fred" starring Sellers, Milligan, and directed by the great Richard Lester?"

I am not usually a big fan of horror films, and have only seen a handful of them (and none of the "Halloween"s or "Friday the Thirteenth"s) - but I can appreciate a frightening horror film not because of gore. And I'm pretty sure this is very scary.

This film is deeply moving; it's poignant. It -is- heartfelt, because AIDS in the early '90s -was- a significant challenge. But its real message is one of resilience.

Mark and Tom were in a long-term, loving relationship. Their commitment to each other is evident right away, and as they face the challenges of AIDS together, their bond becomes the focal point of their lives, showcasing incredible strength.

When "Silverlake Life" was originally released, I was deeply involved in HIV/AIDS education and health care, volunteering as a counselor at an HIV/AIDS clinic. The film resonates like few others of its time could, because Mark and Tom were real people, living the very experiences that I saw on a daily basis in real life. I knew from firsthand experience what it was like to witness people facing AIDS with courage and dignity; seeing Mark and Tom in the film was very much like watching profound love endure. It touched me in a way that, even all these years later, still inspires hope and humanity.
